page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: The second reversal: bupivacaine
sentence_as_it_stands: **The mixture performs like the chloroprocaine, not like the bupivacaine.** Adding the ester cost **139 − 36 = 103 minutes**, a **74%** loss, and the combination was statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine on its own.
quote: Statistical analysis revealed that the difference in … duration of action between bupivacaine alone and … bupivacaine plus chloroprocaine was highly signifi- … cant (p c 0.001), and that the difference in duration … of action between bupivacaine-chloroprocaine mix- … ture and chloroprocaine alone was also significant (p … -=0.01).
corrected_wording: The mixture performs much more like the chloroprocaine than like the bupivacaine. Adding the ester cost 139 − 36 = 103 minutes, a 74% loss. The combination was not statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine on its own: the full text reports that comparison as significant as well (p < 0.01), beside p < 0.001 for the mixture against bupivacaine alone.
notes: The paper's abstract says only that the mixture was 'similar to' chloroprocaine alone; the page upgrades that to a null result, which the Results section contradicts. The same upgrade appears in this page's own source register ('significantly less than bupivacaine alone and statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine alone'), so it needs fixing in both places. The direction matters: the mixture lasted significantly longer than the ester alone, so the amide's contribution was greatly reduced rather than abolished, which bears on this page's 'destroys the amide's duration' wording and on the Ropivacaine page's 'effectively erased'.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: Sources — The other human intradermal measurements (Kim 1979 entry, Limits)
sentence_as_it_stands: **Limits:** abstract read in full; the paper itself is paywalled and the methods section has not been read, so **the injection volume and the concentrations are unknown** — doses are given only in milligrams, and the match to Sweet's [dose figure omitted] is a match of dose, not necessarily of volume or concentration; n=20; a single centre; 1979; the mechanism is the authors' proposal and was not tested.
quote: Using a tuberculin syringe, intradermal wheals … were raised on the volar aspect of each volunteer's … forearm with [dose figure omitted] of three local anesthetic solutions.
corrected_wording: Limits: n=20; a single centre; 1979; the mechanism is the authors' proposal and was not tested; the study is double-blind and paired, each volunteer receiving all three solutions, but it is nowhere stated to be randomised. The full text was read on 2026-10-08 and closes the volume and concentration gap: the methods and the duration table give the concentration of each of the three solutions and the volume injected per wheal, and that volume is the same as Sweet's, so the match to Sweet is a match of concentration and volume as well as of milligram dose.
notes: This is the limit the record itself treats as load-bearing — the sibling bupivacaine-wheals entry says in terms that 'volume is what this page's scaling argument turns on'. With the volume known, the lower anchor of the square-root-of-volume fit is two independent measurements at one volume, one concentration and one endpoint rather than one measurement plus a dose-only match. The volume figure itself is recorded only in the paper card and in the D006 claim update's reason, under the brief's own-question exception.

section: Sources › Duration in skin (Kim 1979 entry, Limits)
sentence_as_it_stands: **Limits:** 1979; healthy volunteers; **the paper states the dose in milligrams and the abstract gives neither the injected volume nor the concentration**, so the milligram dose matches Sweet's while the volume may not, and volume is what this page's scaling argument turns on; the mechanism offered — competition for non-specific binding sites — is the authors' proposal, not a measurement; **chloroprocaine is not procaine**, and no intradermal measurement of procaine mixed with an amide exists.

The full text was read on 2026-10-08: the methods and the duration table give both the concentration of each solution and the volume injected per wheal, and that volume matches Sweet's, so the two studies match on concentration and volume as well as on milligram dose and the scaling argument's lower anchor no longer rests on an inferred volume.

The volume figure is recorded only in the paper card and in the D006 claim update's reason.

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: Sources > What has no source
sentence_as_it_stands: The claim that bupivacaine is the most painful to inject of the seven agents on the comparison page. No study has compared all seven for injection pain intradermally, and the one that is cited for the claim found etidocaine worse.
quote: During these experiments, stinging was a common experience with all test solutions.
corrected_wording: The claim that bupivacaine is the most painful to inject of the seven agents on the comparison page. No study has compared all seven for injection pain intradermally. The study cited for the claim is Howe & Williams 1994 (PMID 8034840), which compared three of them at matched pH and found lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine most; it remains the only pH-matched comparison and has not been corroborated. The only other intradermal comparison of those same three agents recorded injection pain without matching pH and found stinging common to all test solutions, ranking none of them (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776).
notes: The sentence is correct as far as it goes, and the attribution is right: the paper cited for the etidocaine-worse finding is Howe & Williams 1994, not Morgan & Russell 1975 (verified in Europe PMC, EXT_ID:8034840, and against every citing passage in the record). What the sentence does not show is that a second human intradermal comparison of exactly those three agents exists, 19 years earlier, and that it reports injection pain as common to all solutions without separating them. So the one-study ranking is uncorroborated and the only independent look at the same three agents found no difference. Morgan & Russell 1975 is cited nowhere in the record: searches of Notion for the PMID, the DOI, 'Morgan 1975' and the title returned no hit, and the string 'Morgan' does not occur in the bupivacaine, mepivacaine, ropivacaine, comparison, wheal-literature or Reference-register pages.

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: What is still unknown
sentence_as_it_stands: Whether [dose figure omitted] really outlasts [dose figure omitted] in skin. The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration-duration relationship at higher strengths. The full text was not obtainable. What would settle it: reading Aps and Reynolds 1976 in full, or a modern repeat.
quote: The increase in duration of action with increased concentration was greater for bupivacaine and etidocaine as compared with lignocaine.
corrected_wording: Whether a stronger solution really outlasts a weaker one in skin. The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration-duration relationship at higher strengths; the full text was not obtainable. A second, independent human intradermal measurement points the same way as the abstract: in a double-blind weal study in four volunteers, half-recovery of pinprick lengthened with concentration more steeply for bupivacaine and etidocaine than for lignocaine, and the higher of the two bupivacaine strengths tested gave roughly twice the half-recovery time of the lower (76.5 +/- 8.0 min against 40.5 +/- 6.3 min; Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776). Reading Aps and Reynolds 1976 in full would still settle the three-strength question.
notes: The page's own open question is answered in the same direction by a study the page does not hold. Morgan & Russell fitted half-recovery time against log concentration for each agent (their fig. 3) and found the concentration/duration slopes for bupivacaine and etidocaine clearly steeper than lignocaine's, which is the relationship this entry says it cannot settle. Measured in intradermal weals on normal forearm skin in four healthy men, on a half-recovery rather than a full-recovery endpoint, which is why it narrows rather than closes the question. Concentrations are omitted per the brief; only the two duration values and their ratio are given.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? > What a tenfold rise in concentration buys, in skin
sentence_as_it_stands: Willatts fitted a straight line to duration against the logarithm of concentration for each drug. Those slopes are the clearest statement anyone has of what concentration is worth in this tissue.
quote: A log-linear response … was assumed for the two … standard drugs and so only two points were estimated. … Three points are given for etidocaine.
corrected_wording: Willatts fitted a straight line to duration against the logarithm of concentration for each drug, and his is the only such set covering six agents at once. It is not the only set: a 1975 double-blind weal study fitted half-recovery time against log concentration for lignocaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine in four volunteers and found the slopes for bupivacaine and etidocaine clearly steeper than lignocaine's, so bupivacaine joins ropivacaine as an agent whose skin duration does rise appreciably with concentration (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776).
notes: The page says this comparison 'decides more about how to inject than any ranking between drugs in this document', so a second data set bears directly on something practical. The conclusion drawn from Willatts carries its own scope ('For the six drugs Willatts timed') and is not wrong; the page also already flags ropivacaine as an exception. What is overstated is 'the clearest statement anyone has': a second human intradermal concentration-duration data set exists, it covers two drugs on this page (lidocaine/lignocaine and bupivacaine), and for bupivacaine it runs the other way from the six-drug rule. Morgan & Russell's own figures are half-recovery times, not full recovery, and rest on four subjects, so they are a weaker data set than Willatts's - but they are the only concentration-duration figures for intradermal bupivacaine that exist, and the page currently has none.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: Sources — The Reynolds series (Reynolds F, Bryson THL, Nicholas ADG 1976 annotation); and the same paper's row in the seven-papers table
sentence_as_it_stands: Limits: abstract read; full text not indexed and not read. … No durations in minutes are available from the abstract, so the study establishes the absence of a concentration effect but not the durations of the comparators.
quote: TABLE III. Time to full recovery … Time (min) … Agent              n      Mean SEM
corrected_wording: Full text read. Table III tabulates the mean time to full recovery in minutes, with SEM and n, for every agent and concentration: in the first trial lignocaine 65.7 ± 5.3 (n=28), bupivacaine 82.5 ± 8.7 (n=28) and aptocaine 91.3 ± 2.8 pooled (n=167); in the second, prilocaine 78.6 ± 5.1 pooled (n=81), mepivacaine 98.6 ± 4.7 pooled (n=81) and aptocaine 98.9 ± 8.1 (n=27). Times to 50% recovery are given in the text: about 32 min for lignocaine, bupivacaine and prilocaine, 60 min for mepivacaine and aptocaine. The endpoint is a permanent score of 10, that is complete recovery of pinprick sensation over the bleb, tested every 10 min, at [dose figure omitted] per intradermal injection.
notes: This is the correction the rest of the packet turns on. Several pages state that no human intradermal head-to-head gives durations in minutes; this paper does, for five agents, and its full text is readable. Per-concentration means in minutes are also given for mepivacaine and prilocaine.

page: mepivacaine-wheals
section: The recommendation (first bullet)
sentence_as_it_stands: The only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981).
quote: Every 10 min the area of … each bleb was tested five times with a lancet, while the … subject looked away, and the number of times out of … 10 that the prick felt sharp, for each solution, was … recorded. This was continued until sensation had … returned to normal at all sites.
corrected_wording: Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194) measured mepivacaine in human skin by that same test five years earlier — pinprick over an intradermal bleb, tested every 10 min to a permanent score of 10 — in 27 double-blind volunteers at three concentrations, giving mean times to full recovery of 97.0, 95.2 and 103.7 min (98.6 min pooled, n=81) and 60 min to 50% recovery. Three studies, not one, have measured mepivacaine in human skin by that test (Reynolds 1976; Fairley and Reynolds 1981; Willatts and Reynolds 1985), and all three put it under two hours.
notes: This is the page's headline recommendation sentence and the lead the S1 task flagged. The page's conclusion that mepivacaine is not a longer wheal survives; the uniqueness claim does not. The 1976 method section says of the second trial 'Exactly the same procedure was followed', so the pinprick-over-bleb method quoted here covers the mepivacaine arm.

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: What is still unknown ('Whether the square-root scaling holds'); and Why the eight-hour figure does not apply to a wheal / Sources › Duration in skin, where Sweet 1982 is called the governing number
sentence_as_it_stands: Whether the square-root scaling holds. The 60-minute estimate for a [dose figure omitted] wheal is an interpolation between two studies that differ in tissue layer, endpoint and country.
quote: The mean time to full recovery (permanent score of … 10) was calculated for each agent and is shown in table Ilia. The mean duration to full recovery for … aptocaine (all solutions) was significantly longer than … for lignocaine (P< 0.001) but not for bupivacaine.
corrected_wording: A third human intradermal measurement sits between the two the estimate interpolates from. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed plain bupivacaine in 28 double-blind volunteers, in skin, at a wheal volume, to complete recovery of pinprick sensation: mean 82.5 min (SEM 8.7). It shares the endpoint and the tissue layer with Sweet 1982 at half Sweet's volume, so the step between those two volumes can be read from measurement rather than interpolated.
notes: The page's own 'What would settle it' asks for wheals of three volumes timed side by side; two of the three now have a measurement with the same endpoint in the same tissue layer. Reynolds 1976 is not cited anywhere on this page.

page: Ropivacaine Wheals
section: The comparability argument ('The duration comparisons are at unmatched concentrations and in unmatched tissues')
sentence_as_it_stands: Only Cederholm 1994 compares two drugs at matched concentration, matched volume and matched route, and the two drugs are ropivacaine and bupivacaine
quote: Exactly the same procedure was followed. … Twenty-seven volunteers, aged 20-51 yr, seven of … whom participated in the previous study, received the … following seven solutions:
corrected_wording: Cederholm 1994 is not the only study comparing two drugs at matched concentration, matched volume and matched route. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) compared mepivacaine and prilocaine at three matched concentrations each, at the same intradermal volume and by the same route, in the same 27 volunteers in one session, timing duration to complete recovery: mepivacaine 98.6 ± 4.7 min pooled against prilocaine 78.6 ± 5.1 min, the difference significant at P<0.01. Cederholm remains the only matched comparison that includes ropivacaine.
notes: The page uses this sentence to argue that the duration comparisons cannot be ranked against each other. A matched-concentration, matched-volume, same-subject human intradermal duration comparison of two marketed agents does exist.

page: Ropivacaine Wheals
section: 9a.5 Mepivacaine — the drug nobody in this project has considered ('Would not: duration')
sentence_as_it_stands: Block potency 1.5 against ropivacaine’s 6, and in Willatts & Reynolds every mepivacaine bleb had fully recovered within 80 minutes.
quote: Mepivacaine [dose figure omitted]           27       97.0 ±9.0 … 27       95.2 ±7.6 … 103.7 ±7.7 … all       81       98.6 ±4.7
corrected_wording: Willatts and Reynolds tested mepivacaine only up to the lowest of the strengths in clinical use, so 80 minutes is not its ceiling. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed mepivacaine at three higher concentrations intradermally in 27 volunteers, giving mean times to complete recovery of 97.0, 95.2 and 103.7 min, 98.6 min pooled. Mepivacaine is still an intermediate-duration drug in skin, but the figure to use at the strengths actually sold is around 100 minutes rather than under 80.
notes: The page's own limit note on Willatts says its top mepivacaine concentration is well below the strength sold; Reynolds 1976 fills exactly that gap, and the 9a.5 assessment of mepivacaine as an option rests on the 80-minute figure.

page: What is still unsettled across these pages, and what would settle each one
section: Sources › The unopened intradermal literature (Willatts & Reynolds annotation)
sentence_as_it_stands: The paper reports slopes, not absolute minutes — per-concentration means exist only inside a figure. The 80-minute statement is a single sentence about complete recovery, not a set of per-concentration means.
quote: TABLE III. Time to full recovery … Time (min) … Agent              n      Mean SEM
corrected_wording: Per-concentration means in absolute minutes do exist elsewhere in the same series. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) tabulates the mean time to full recovery in minutes, with SEM and n, for mepivacaine and prilocaine at each of three concentrations and for lignocaine and bupivacaine at one each: lignocaine 65.7, bupivacaine 82.5, prilocaine 78.6 pooled and mepivacaine 98.6 pooled. The paper is not in this page's source list.
notes: This page exists to point at the highest-value missing material, and the item it names as missing — absolute per-concentration minutes in human skin — is available in a paper already cited elsewhere in the record whose full text had not been read.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? (duration table, prilocaine row, 'With epinephrine' column, and the 'What the figure rests on' cell)
sentence_as_it_stands: Prilocaine | under 80 min up to [dose figure omitted] | not measured in skin | 10 volunteers, intradermal
corrected_wording: Prilocaine with adrenaline has been timed in skin: 288.7 min of analgesia and 349.1 min of hypoaesthesia in 20 female volunteers given intradermal weals under double-blind conditions (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413), against 99.1 min and 172.9 min for the same solution plain.
notes: This is the cell claim D009 was taken from, and it is the only cell in the table's 'With epinephrine' column that says nothing was measured. The paper's Table I is captioned 'Duration of effect of solutions with (*) and without adrenaline (mean and SE)' and the starred prilocaine row carries both timed endpoints. The 'What the figure rests on' cell should also name this 20-volunteer study alongside the 10-volunteer one.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? / Four things about that table
sentence_as_it_stands: **So four of the seven drugs here have been timed in human skin to complete recovery, and all four ran short.** ... **Everything measured in skin at a wheal volume is short; the long figures in circulation come from larger volumes or other tissues.**
quote: found to give significantly longer analgesia than prilocaine and significantly longer hypo-
corrected_wording: Not every intradermal timing to complete recovery in human skin is short. A double-blind volunteer trial timed bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine as intradermal weals to the point at which the sensory change had completely disappeared, and plain bupivacaine ran 306.8 min at single and 435.8 min at double strength, with plain lignocaine at 221.1 min (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The weal volume in the 1970 trial, [dose figure omitted] per weal, is above the [dose figure omitted] range this page means by a wheal, so the second sentence's 'at a wheal volume' qualifier survives; the first sentence, which carries no volume qualifier, does not. Six drug-strength combinations were timed to complete recovery there, which also raises the count of drugs with such a figure.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? (duration table, bupivacaine row) and 'The bupivacaine spread is explained by volume'
sentence_as_it_stands: Bupivacaine | [dose figure omitted]; about 60 min at [dose figure omitted] | around 7 h | 20 volunteers at [dose figure omitted]; the wheal-sized figure interpolated, not measured; the 8 h figure is [dose figure omitted] under the skin
quote: found to give significantly longer analgesia than prilocaine and significantly longer hypo-
corrected_wording: A third intradermal measurement of plain bupivacaine exists, at a weal volume close to the smaller of the two points this interpolation uses: 199.5 min to the return of some sensation and 306.8 min to complete recovery, in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, with the double-strength solution at 252.8 min and 435.8 min (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The 60-minute wheal figure is derived from a two-point square-root-of-volume fit. The 1970 figures sit at a volume only slightly above the lower of those two points yet are 1.6 to 2.5 times its duration, so the fit does not hold and the interpolated figure is not supported by the data it is drawn from. This is the same defect as the bupivacaine-wheals page finding, recorded separately because it is a different page.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? (duration table, lidocaine row, 'With epinephrine' column and its 'What the figure rests on' cell)
sentence_as_it_stands: Lidocaine | under 80 min up to [dose figure omitted]; 80 min to 2 h at [dose figure omitted] | about 2 h, self-measured | the intradermal figure from 10 volunteers; the [dose figure omitted] and the with-epinephrine figures both self-measured by a single user in neuropathic leg skin, not from a trial; the dose-response trials predict 2 h 40 to 6 h and the self-measurement came in below all of it
quote: Adrenaline significantly lengthened the action of all three drugs, this prolongation being greatest with lignocaine.
corrected_wording: A published intradermal figure for lignocaine with adrenaline in human skin exists: 416.2 min to the return of some sensation and 483.8 min to complete recovery, in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, against 127.6 min and 221.1 min for the same solution plain (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The cell currently rests on a single user's own measurement in neuropathic leg skin, with the note saying the with-epinephrine figure is 'not from a trial'. A trial figure in healthy forearm skin now exists, and it falls above the 2 h 40 to 6 h range the page says the dose-response trials predict. The tissue differs from neuropathic leg skin, which is the page's own stated reason for the gap.

page: prilocaine-wheals
section: How long does it actually last?
sentence_as_it_stands: **In skin, the one head-to-head measurement in minutes gives a large advantage — in horses.**
quote: found to give significantly longer analgesia than prilocaine and significantly longer hypo-
corrected_wording: A human head-to-head measurement in minutes on a skin endpoint exists: a double-blind trial timed prilocaine against bupivacaine and lignocaine as intradermal weals in the same 20 female volunteers and reported mean durations in minutes with standard errors and significance tests between agents (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: This is claim C066. The horse study remains the only one giving confidence intervals, and it remains a nerve block rather than a weal, but it is not the only head-to-head duration measurement in minutes on a skin endpoint. In the 1970 trial prilocaine was the shortest of the three agents on both endpoints, plain and with adrenaline.

page: prilocaine-wheals
section: Sources — What has no source
sentence_as_it_stands: - **No measurement of how long a prilocaine wheal lasts in human skin.** The duration section reasons across four studies, none of which used this route in this tissue.
corrected_wording: A measurement of how long a prilocaine weal lasts in human skin exists: 99.1 min of analgesia and 172.9 min of hypoaesthesia plain, 100.8 min and 244.5 min at double strength, and 288.7 min and 349.1 min with adrenaline, in 20 female volunteers given intradermal weals under double-blind conditions (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The bullet is wrong twice. It contradicts this page's own duration section, which describes Willatts and Reynolds 1985 as intradermal in human volunteers, and it is refuted outright by the 1970 trial, which gives means in minutes per concentration and is the figure the page says has no source.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: What is still unknown
sentence_as_it_stands: **Whether plain and adrenalized lidocaine differ in skin by the factor the dental literature claims.** Your own measurement is about **1.3×**, with the blanching visibly outlasting the analgesia; the literature figure is two to three times. *What would settle it:* Swerdlow and Jones 1970, which measured exactly that comparison intradermally, with saline controls, in 1970. It remains unretrieved.
quote: Adrenaline significantly lengthened the action of all three drugs, this prolongation being greatest with lignocaine.
corrected_wording: The paper has been read and it does measure that comparison intradermally. For lignocaine the adrenalized-to-plain ratio is 3.26 on time to the return of some sensation (416.2 against 127.6 min) and 2.19 on time to complete recovery (483.8 against 221.1 min), in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, and the prolongation was greatest with lignocaine of the three agents tested (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The open question is answered: the two-to-three-times figure is reproduced intradermally in healthy forearm skin, at the upper end on the earlier endpoint and inside the range on complete recovery. The 1.3x figure beside it is the page owner's own measurement in neuropathic leg skin and is marked as his own use, not research; this finding corrects only the literature side. Corresponding ratios were 2.91 and 2.02 for prilocaine and 2.15 and 1.63 for bupivacaine.

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: What a wheal of your own size would give / Why the eight-hour figure does not apply to a wheal
sentence_as_it_stands: The two measurements above are the only two points available, and they can be joined.
quote: found to give significantly longer analgesia than prilocaine and significantly longer hypo-
corrected_wording: A third intradermal measurement of plain bupivacaine is available, at a weal volume close to the smaller of those two points: 199.5 min to the return of some sensation and 306.8 min to complete recovery, with the double-strength solution at 252.8 min and 435.8 min, in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The square-root-of-volume fit, the roughly 60-minute wheal estimate, and the conclusion that bupivacaine at wheal size sits at or below what plain lidocaine gives all rest on there being only two points. The third point is at a volume only slightly above the lower of the two and runs 1.6 to 2.5 times its duration, which breaks the fit rather than extending it. The page's '[dose figure omitted] intradermal wheals' measurement and this one also disagree with each other by a wide margin, which widens the stated uncertainty.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: The second reversal: bupivacaine (also the Kim 1979 source-register entry)
sentence_as_it_stands: **The same 1979 paper settles a question nobody had answered: whether an ester and an amide can share a syringe.**
quote: A review of previous studies of local anes- … thetic mixtures used for this purpose indicates that … while rapid onset has bem a consistent finding, the … duration of action has been inconsistent.
corrected_wording: The same 1979 paper answers for skin a question that had already been asked in other tissues. Its own introduction reviews a prior literature of local anaesthetic mixture studies and reports their results on duration as inconsistent, and it cites a 1974 human comparison of a chloroprocaine-plus-bupivacaine mixture against bupivacaine alone in brachial plexus block, with mean duration of motor blockade for each (Cunningham 1974, PMID 4429221). A 1977 study of compounded chloroprocaine-plus-bupivacaine mixtures in 48 patients, epidural and brachial plexus, is in the same reference list (Raj 1977, PMID 556897). What is new in 1979 is the intradermal route.
notes: This is claim C033, re-judged narrowed → refuted. The same framing appears in this page's source-register entry for the paper ('the answer to whether an ester and an amide can share a syringe') and on the 'What is still unsettled' page ('which bears on whether an ester and an amide can be mixed'). Both deciding studies are in the 1979 paper's own reference list. Cunningham 1974 has no abstract on record (engine: amass, before the usage limit); the Raj 1977 abstract was read on Europe PMC.

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: Sources › Duration in skin (the Sweet 1982 entry, 'The figure has been measured twice')
sentence_as_it_stands: **The figure has been measured twice.** Kim, Goto and Arakawa put the same **[dose figure omitted]** of bupivacaine into the skin of 20 volunteers three years earlier, double-blind, and measured **139 ± 78 minutes** against Sweet's **125 ± 70** — two laboratories, one milligram dose, means **11 percent** apart, and both standard deviations more than half their mean.
quote: Following … the injections, analgesia to pinprick on the injection … site was determined every 10 minutes until full recov- … ery occurred.
corrected_wording: The figure has been measured twice, and the two measurements agree on more than the dose. Kim, Goto and Arakawa put bupivacaine into the skin of 20 volunteers three years earlier, double-blind, and measured 139 ± 78 minutes against Sweet's 125 ± 70 — two laboratories, means 11 percent apart, both standard deviations more than half their mean. The full text shows the two also match on concentration, on injected volume, on the number of volunteers, on the design and on the endpoint: like Sweet, Kim timed pinprick analgesia to full recovery of sensation, measured from the moment of injection to the last reported analgesia at the site.
notes: The page calls the agreement 'one milligram dose, two laboratories'; the full text makes it a much closer replication. It also fixes Kim's endpoint, which matters because this page and its siblings sort every duration figure by endpoint — complete analgesia, half recovery or full recovery — and Kim's endpoint was not previously known. Bears on claims D006 and D008.

page: Ropivacaine Wheals
section: 9.1 The intradermal experiment, in humans (and 15.5 Mixing, source register)
sentence_as_it_stands: `ABSTRACT-ONLY` **Kim, Goto & Arakawa 1979**, *Anesth Analg*, DOI 10.1213/00000539-197909000-00003. Double-blind trial in **20 human volunteers**, intradermal:
quote: A double-blind study was performed on 20 healthy … young volunteers.
corrected_wording: Kim, Goto & Arakawa 1979, Anesth Analg 58:364–366, PMID 573558, DOI 10.1213/00000539-197909000-00003. Full text read 2026-10-08. Double-blind, paired trial in 20 healthy young human volunteers, intradermal: each volunteer received all three solutions as separate wheals on the volar forearm, raised with a tuberculin syringe, and the three durations were compared by paired Student's t test. The endpoint was complete recovery — pinprick analgesia tested every 10 minutes until full recovery, with duration timed from injection to the last reported analgesia at the site. The methods give the concentration of each solution and the volume per wheal. The paper is nowhere stated to be randomised.
notes: All three duration figures in the table on this page (139 ± 78, 24 ± 11 and 36 ± 16 minutes, mean ± 1 SD) are confirmed verbatim against the full text, as is the attribution of the proposed mechanism. The ABSTRACT-ONLY provenance tag here and the ABSTRACT tag on the 15.5 Mixing register entry can both be upgraded. The design facts added — paired within-subject, complete-recovery endpoint, stated volume and concentration, no randomisation — were not available from the abstract.

sentence_as_it_stands: Mean ± 1 SD. **The mixture's duration was significantly less than bupivacaine alone, and similar to chloroprocaine alone.** The long-acting amide's contribution was effectively erased.

The same misreading appears in a stronger form on the sibling wheal-literature page as 'statistically indistinguishable' (finding F001).

page: Ropivacaine Wheals
section: 9.1 The intradermal experiment, in humans
sentence_as_it_stands: This is human, intradermal, double-blind, and it confirms the 139 → 36 figure the project was carrying. **It is the single most transferable mixing result available** — the only one in the right tissue by the right route.
corrected_wording: This is human, intradermal, double-blind, and it confirms the 139 → 36 figure the project was carrying. It is the only human intradermal measurement of an ester mixed with an amide. It is not the only human intradermal mixing measurement: Sweet 1982 (PMID 6751499) compared plain intradermal bupivacaine with bupivacaine–lidocaine mixtures in 20 volunteers, double-blind, and Collins 2013 (PMID 24431939) compared intradermal mixtures of bupivacaine and lidocaine with epinephrine in 25 subjects, randomised and double-blind — both amide with amide, which is the pairing Part VI is about for ropivacaine with lidocaine.
notes: No sentence in Kim 1979 bears on this, so the quote is empty per the brief's rule. The evidence is Sweet 1982 (PMID 6751499, already in this record's own register on bupivacaine-wheals: 20 volunteers, double-blind, intradermal wheals on the volar forearm, pinprick to full recovery) and Collins 2013 (PMID 24431939, abstract read: 'Twenty-five subjects were enrolled in a double-blinded, randomized block design study to evaluate the onset and duration of four different mixtures of lidocaine and bupivacaine with epinephrine'; 'Four intradermal injections were made in the volar forearms of each participant'). Neither is cited anywhere on the Ropivacaine Wheals page, so section 9.1 was written without them in view. Engine: amass (Collins record), before the usage limit.

page: The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: Why does this literature exist, and why do the reviews miss it?
sentence_as_it_stands: That tradition is small, old and British, and the reviews do not read it. The core of it is five papers from one anesthetic unit at St Thomas' Hospital in London between 1976 and 1985, plus a scatter of American dermatology and anesthesia papers between 1952 and 1994.
quote: Probably … the least variation occurs when using … intradermal … weals, and this technique has been used to … compare local anaesthetic activity in both animals … and man.
corrected_wording: That tradition is small, old and British, and the reviews do not read it. Its core is five papers from one anaesthetic unit at St Thomas' Hospital in London between 1976 and 1985, plus a scatter of American dermatology and anesthesia papers between 1952 and 1994, plus at least one British volunteer weal study from a second London unit outside both groups: a double-blind intradermal weal comparison of lignocaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine in four volunteers at Hammersmith Hospital and the Royal Postgraduate Medical School (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776). That paper in turn cites human weal work from 1936 (Sinha, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 57:199) and 1956 (Geddes, PMID 13293283), so the tradition runs back further than 1952.
notes: This page is the record's register of the intradermal weal literature and names the gap it exists to fill, so an uncited member of that literature matters here more than elsewhere. Morgan & Russell 1975 is a Hammersmith paper, not St Thomas', and predates the 1976 start of the Reynolds series; it is absent from this page and from every other page checked. The 1936 and 1956 antecedents it names are its own citations, not papers read here: no Europe PMC record exists for Sinha 1936, and Geddes 1956 has a Europe PMC citation but no abstract.

Morgan & Russell 1975 used the same intradermal volume on the same forearm site and tested plain bupivacaine at two strengths seven years earlier, on a half-recovery rather than a full-recovery endpoint. The endpoint difference is why this narrows the limit rather than removing it: the two studies are not interchangeable anchors for the smaller-volume point the page's volume-scaling arithmetic rests on.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each one cost in injection pain?
sentence_as_it_stands: Bupivacaine is not the most painful drug in this group, and the study usually cited for that says the opposite. The pH-matched intradermal comparison of plain lidocaine, plain bupivacaine and plain etidocaine - every solution adjusted to pH 5.95 +/- 0.15 so that acidity could not do the explaining - reports in its own words that "lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine hurt most", which puts bupivacaine in the middle of the three. It tested three of the seven drugs here, so it cannot rank bupivacaine against the other four in either direction.
quote: During these experiments, stinging was a common experience with all test solutions.
corrected_wording: Bupivacaine is not the most painful drug in this group, and the study usually cited for that says the opposite. The pH-matched intradermal comparison of plain lidocaine, plain bupivacaine and plain etidocaine - every solution adjusted to pH 5.95 +/- 0.15 so that acidity could not do the explaining - reports in its own words that "lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine hurt most", which puts bupivacaine in the middle of the three. It tested three of the seven drugs here, so it cannot rank bupivacaine against the other four in either direction, and it is the only study to have ranked them: the one other intradermal comparison of the same three agents reported stinging as common to all test solutions and separated none of them (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776).
notes: The passage is accurate about Howe & Williams 1994 and the ordering is verified in Europe PMC. The addition is that the ordering stands on a single trial: the only other intradermal volunteer comparison of lignocaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine recorded injection pain and found it common to all solutions, without ranking them. That study did not match or report pH, so it does not displace the pH-matched comparison - it means the ranking is uncorroborated rather than contradicted. Recorded on this page as well as on bupivacaine-wheals because the ranking table and the injection-pain column live here.

sentence_as_it_stands: Two studies have measured this, four years apart, from the same laboratory, and they agree. … Between them they cover 33 volunteers, and neither found a mepivacaine bleb lasting more than two hours.
quote: Mepivacaine [dose figure omitted]           27       97.0 ±9.0 … 27       95.2 ±7.6 … 103.7 ±7.7 … all       81       98.6 ±4.7
corrected_wording: Three studies have measured this, from the same laboratory over nine years, and they agree. Between them they cover 60 volunteers, and none found a mepivacaine bleb lasting more than about 1.7 hours — the longest group mean in the earliest of them, Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194), being 103.7 ± 7.7 min.
notes: Reynolds 1976 adds 27 volunteers and is the earliest of the three, not a later one; the page's substantive conclusion is unchanged and in fact strengthened.

page: mepivacaine-wheals
section: Sources › Skin: vessels and duration (Willatts & Reynolds 1985 annotation)
sentence_as_it_stands: The second intradermal measurement of mepivacaine, and the only one that times it against lidocaine and prilocaine in the same volunteers.
quote: Exactly the same procedure was followed. … Twenty-seven volunteers, aged 20-51 yr, seven of … whom participated in the previous study, received the … following seven solutions:
corrected_wording: The third intradermal measurement of mepivacaine, and the only one that times it against lidocaine and prilocaine together in the same volunteers. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed mepivacaine against prilocaine in the same 27 volunteers in one session, but lignocaine was injected in a separate earlier trial in a different group of 28, so Reynolds 1976 is not a mepivacaine-versus-lidocaine comparison in the same subjects.
notes: The point the S1 task asked to settle. Reynolds 1976 ran two trials with different subject groups (seven subjects overlapped): trial 1 was lignocaine, bupivacaine and aptocaine in the same 28 subjects; trial 2 was mepivacaine, prilocaine and aptocaine in the same 27. No agent except aptocaine crosses the two trials, so any 'same volunteers' comparison drawn from this paper must stay inside one trial.

quote: TABLE III. Time to full recovery … Time (min) … Agent              n      Mean SEM
corrected_wording: Duration in human skin has been measured three times. The earliest, Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194), used a full-recovery endpoint — a permanent score of 10 on pinprick over the bleb — on the flexor forearms of volunteers aged 20 to 51, giving 98.6 ± 4.7 min pooled for mepivacaine (n=81). What is still unmeasured is a mepivacaine wheal in neuropathic leg skin.
notes: Two errors in one sentence: 'measured once' and 'at half-recovery rather than full block'. A full-recovery endpoint in human skin does exist for mepivacaine. The page's 'What would settle it' — a same-day leg-against-leg comparison — remains unmet.

sentence_as_it_stands: The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration–duration relationship at higher strengths. The full text was not obtainable.
quote: there is no significant difference in duration … between the three different concentrations of … mepivacaine and prilocaine.
corrected_wording: A separate Reynolds-group paper from the same year and the same journal volume bears on this without settling it: Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194, Br J Anaesth 48:347-354, a different paper from Aps and Reynolds at 48:1171-1174) tested three concentrations each of three agents intradermally in human volunteers and found no significant difference in duration between them, which matches the authors' later description of a flat concentration-duration relationship at the higher strengths. It gave bupivacaine at one concentration only, so the question of the two bupivacaine strengths is still open.
notes: Also a citation hazard worth recording: there are two Reynolds-group 1976 papers in Br J Anaesth volume 48 — the aptocaine intradermal trial at 48:347 and Aps and Reynolds on concentration and vasoactivity at 48:1171. They should not be conflated.

Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) found no significant difference in mepivacaine duration across the three higher concentrations it tested, so the slope flattens above the range the figure comes from, and carrying it up to the strengths on sale overstates what extra concentration buys.

page: prilocaine-wheals

sentence_as_it_stands: Longer than lidocaine in direction, and small in size once the tissue is right. Five measurements put numbers on it and they do not agree with each other, which is itself the finding. The one taken in human skin at a wheal volume is the one that decides it, and it is short.

corrected_wording: A further measurement in human skin puts numbers on it and does not agree with the others: in intradermal weals in the same 20 volunteers, prilocaine was shorter than lignocaine on both timed endpoints, plain and with adrenaline, and the difference between the two agents was not statistically significant on either endpoint (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).

Its point estimates run against the 'longer than lidocaine in direction' opening, while its significance test agrees with the page's own conclusion that the two are the same drug for practical purposes here.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: The seven papers nobody has pulled (item 1) and Sources — The retrieval queue
sentence_as_it_stands: **Swerdlow & Jones 1970.** *The duration of action of bupivacaine, prilocaine and lignocaine.* Br J Anaesth 42(4):335–9. PMID 4913413. **The broadest early comparison, and still unread.** ... **Limits: entirely unread. No abstract exists** — PubMed and Europe PMC both return "abstract not available," the full-text index carries no readable text, and the publisher's copy is behind a robots block and a captcha. Four retrieval routes were tried and all four failed. Nothing about its numbers is known.
quote: The duration of analgesia and of hypoaesthesia produced by a variety of solutions has been examined by skin weal testing; each separate study was carried out in twenty female volunteers under double-blind conditions.
corrected_wording: The paper has now been read in full. It is four successive double-blind trials of 20 female volunteers each, timing intradermal skin weals on the ventral left forearm to the return of some sensation and to complete recovery: bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine each with and without adrenaline; the same three agents with adrenaline from hospital-prepared multidose vials against commercial ampoules; the three agents at double strength; and intradermal saline with and without adrenaline (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
notes: The MeSH-based inference in this entry is confirmed: three drugs with and without adrenaline, intradermally, with a saline comparison - though the saline arm was a fourth separate trial in 20 further nurses rather than a placebo arm inside the main comparison. The design is a within-subject double-blind trial with allocation by random code, not a randomised parallel-group trial, and the subjects were healthy volunteers rather than patients. The count in 'The recommendation' and in 'The seven papers nobody has pulled' is now six unopened rather than seven.

sentence_as_it_stands: **Seven intradermal papers never pulled.** Swerdlow & Jones, *Br J Anaesth* 1970;42(4):335–9 — intradermal bupivacaine, prilocaine and lignocaine with and without adrenaline, the broadest early comparison, no PubMed abstract;
quote: First, bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine were compared with and without
corrected_wording: Six of those seven remain unpulled. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 has been read: it times intradermal bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine each with and without adrenaline in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, and reports mean durations in minutes with standard errors for both of its timed endpoints (PMID 4913413).

page: bupivacaine-wheals
section: Why the eight-hour figure does not apply to a wheal ('And with epinephrine in skin it is about seven hours')
sentence_as_it_stands: **And with epinephrine in skin it is about seven hours.** Collins, Song and Mahabir (2013) gave 25 subjects four intradermal solutions on the volar forearm, all containing epinephrine.
quote: Adrenaline significantly lengthened the action of all three drugs, this prolongation being greatest with lignocaine.
corrected_wording: An independent intradermal measurement agrees: bupivacaine with adrenaline ran 428.6 min to the return of some sensation and 500.2 min to complete recovery in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413), which brackets the 2013 figure.

page: Small Fiber Neuropathy — Intradermal vs. Subcutaneous Injection Routing Analysis
section: Why vasoconstrictors are used, and why they are the wrong thing to reason from; Sources — The depot and how fast it empties
sentence_as_it_stands: Lidocaine with epinephrine gave about **2 hours** — a multiplier of about **1.3**, against the **two to three times** the published skin studies predict.
quote: highly significant for each of the three drugs, both
corrected_wording: The two-to-three-times figure now has a direct intradermal source: for lignocaine the adrenalized-to-plain ratio was 3.26 on time to the return of some sensation and 2.19 on time to complete recovery, in 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, and the increase was highly significant for each of the three agents tested (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).

The same page calls Willatts and Reynolds 1985 'the governing duration figure for anything placed in the dermis'; the 1970 trial's plain intradermal durations are two to four times Willatts' 80-minute recovery ceiling at a larger weal volume, so that description holds at the volume and strengths Willatts used rather than for the dermis generally. The 1.3x figure is the page owner's own measurement in neuropathic leg skin, not research, and is not corrected here.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: What does raising the concentration actually buy? (the 'second study, in five times as many people' paragraph)
sentence_as_it_stands: Going from [dose figure omitted] to [dose figure omitted] is 0.48 of a tenfold step, so on the 1985 slopes it should buy 11 minutes for prilocaine and 15 for mepivacaine — differences too small to surface against between-subject variation

From the lowest to the highest concentration tested the observed change was +11.5 min for prilocaine (76.3 to 87.8 min) and +6.7 min for mepivacaine (97.0 to 103.7 min), against the 11 and 15 minutes the 1985 slopes predict, with SEMs of 8 to 9 min.
